newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish devaluation seen unchanged to Q4 - paper.
newsitem.headline: Polish devaluation seen unchanged to Q4 - paper.

text.p: Poland's Finance Ministry sees the zloty's monthly devaluation rate staying unchanged until at least the end of the third quarter this year, Rzeczpospolita daily on Saturday quoted a ministry official as saying.
Witold Skrok told the newspaper the ministry's assumptions for next year's budget contained a forecast for exchange rate policy.

"There we foresee that until the third quarter of this year inclusively the present currency policy will be implemented," said Skrok, deputy director of the ministry's Finance Policy and Analysis department.
"In the fourth quarter of the year and the first half of 1998 the pace of the crawling peg devaluation would be lower," Skrok said.
The zloty is now devalued by one percent a month against a basket of five Western currencies to compensate for the still high inflation, at 14.6 percent in year-on-year terms in May.

On Thursday, Finance Minister Marek Belka told Reuters Poland was considering a slower pace of monthly zloty devaluations to help curb inflation, saying, "We are starting to think about the decelerating of the crawl."
But he declined to state when this might happen.
The crawling devaluation, the rate of which is set by the independent National Bank of Poland, was last cut on January 8, 1996, by 0.2 point.
Rzeczpospolita quoted Witold Kozinski, the bank's deputy president, as saying that although the devaluation contributed to inflation, any change would have to be carefully considered.
"We must weigh on the one hand the desire to counteract inflation, and on the other the need to restrain speculative capital and the growth of the trade deficit," Kozinski said.
"This means there is a need to keep the rate of the devaluation at the monthly level of one percent," the paper quoted him as saying.

Poland's trade deficit is expected to grow to $12 billion this year or about 5-6 percent of GDP. The central bank has warned it could reach about 7-8 percent of GDP next year if Poland failed to tighten reins on booming investment and consumer demand to stem imports growth. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
